purpose: Atezolizumab is a cancer-fighting medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including certain lung cancers, liver cancer, breast cancer, and bladder cancer. It is often used when other treatments have not worked or alongside other cancer medicines. Your doctor chose this medication because it may help slow or stop your cancer from growing.
how_it_works: Your immune system has natural 'brakes' that cancer cells can hijack to hide from your body's defenses. Atezolizumab works by blocking a protein called PD-L1, which essentially releases those brakes. This allows your own immune system to recognize and attack the cancer cells more effectively.
common_side_effects: Feeling very tired or weak, nausea, decreased appetite, fever, joint or muscle pain, shortness of breath, cough, rash, itching, constipation or diarrhea, and urinary tract infections are among the most commonly reported side effects.
warnings: Because this medicine boosts your immune system, it can sometimes cause your immune system to attack healthy organs — a serious concern. Watch for and report immediately: severe or worsening cough or breathing problems, severe diarrhea, abdominal pain, yellowing of skin or eyes, severe rash, unusual weight gain, or any new symptoms. Infusion reactions can also occur during treatment. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby.
typical_dosing: Atezolizumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into a vein at a clinic or infusion center — you cannot take it as a pill at home. A common dose is 1,200 mg given every 3 weeks, or 840 mg every 2 weeks, depending on your specific cancer and treatment plan. Your first infusion takes about 60 minutes; if tolerated well, later infusions may be shorter. Your doctor will determine the exact schedule that is right for you.
